title: Logic & Proof
content:
KEY CONCEPTS: Discrete math studies distinct, separate values — the mathematics of computation. Propositional logic: statements that are true or false, combined with AND (∧), OR (∨), NOT (¬), IMPLIES (→). Truth tables evaluate compound statements. Logical equivalences (De Morgan's laws: ¬(A∧B) = ¬A∨¬B). Predicate logic adds quantifiers: ∀ (for all), ∃ (there exists). Proof techniques: direct proof, proof by contradiction, proof by contrapositive, and mathematical induction (prove base case, then that each case implies the next — like dominoes).

WORKED EXAMPLE: Prove that if n² is even, then n is even, by contrapositive: assume n is odd (n=2k+1), then n² = 4k²+4k+1 = 2(2k²+2k)+1, which is odd. Since 'n odd → n² odd' is proven, its contrapositive 'n² even → n even' holds. Contrapositive proof turns a hard direct proof into an easy one — a core technique of rigorous reasoning.

PRACTICE: 1) Build a truth table for A → B. 2) State De Morgan's laws. 3) Explain how mathematical induction works.

title: Sets, Relations & Functions
content:
KEY CONCEPTS: A set is a collection of distinct objects. Operations: union (∪), intersection (∩), complement, difference. Subsets and power sets (2ⁿ subsets for n elements). Venn diagrams visualize relationships. Cartesian products form ordered pairs. Relations connect elements; properties: reflexive, symmetric, transitive (equivalence relations partition sets). Functions map each input to exactly one output; injective (one-to-one), surjective (onto), bijective (both — enabling inverses). Cardinality measures set size, including the profound result that some infinities are larger than others (Cantor).

WORKED EXAMPLE: A set with 3 elements {a,b,c} has 2³ = 8 subsets (including the empty set and itself). The power set grows exponentially — this exponential explosion is why many computational problems become intractable as size grows, connecting set theory directly to computational complexity. Counting subsets correctly is foundational to combinatorics and algorithm analysis.

PRACTICE: 1) Find the union and intersection of {1,2,3} and {2,3,4}. 2) Count the subsets of a 4-element set. 3) Explain what makes a function bijective.

title: Combinatorics & Counting
content:
KEY CONCEPTS: Combinatorics counts arrangements and selections. The multiplication principle (independent choices multiply). Permutations (order matters): n!/(n−r)! ways to arrange r of n. Combinations (order doesn't matter): C(n,r) = n!/(r!(n−r)!). The binomial theorem expands (a+b)ⁿ using combinations (Pascal's triangle). The pigeonhole principle (n+1 items in n boxes forces a shared box) proves surprising results. Inclusion-exclusion counts overlapping sets. Counting is the foundation of probability, algorithm analysis, and cryptography.

WORKED EXAMPLE: How many 5-card poker hands from 52 cards? Order doesn't matter, so it's C(52,5) = 52!/(5!·47!) = 2,598,960. This single combination calculation determines every poker probability. Distinguishing when order matters (permutations) from when it doesn't (combinations) is the crucial skill — getting it wrong is the most common counting error.

PRACTICE: 1) Compute C(6,2). 2) How many ways to arrange 4 books on a shelf? 3) Apply the pigeonhole principle: how many people guarantee two share a birth month?

title: Number Theory
content:
KEY CONCEPTS: Number theory studies integers. Divisibility, the Euclidean algorithm for greatest common divisor (GCD). Prime numbers and the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic (unique factorization). Modular arithmetic ('clock math' — remainders): a ≡ b (mod n). Congruences and their properties. Fermat's Little Theorem and Euler's theorem. Number theory, once considered 'pure,' now underpins modern cryptography — RSA encryption relies on the difficulty of factoring large numbers, securing nearly all internet communication.

WORKED EXAMPLE: In modular arithmetic, 17 mod 5 = 2 (17 = 3×5 + 2). Clock arithmetic works this way: 15:00 + 4 hours = 19:00, but on a 12-hour clock, 15 mod 12 = 3, so it's 3 + 4 = 7 o'clock. RSA encryption uses modular exponentiation on huge numbers — the same modular arithmetic, scaled up, is what keeps your online banking secure. Pure number theory became the foundation of digital security.

title: Graph Theory
content:
KEY CONCEPTS: A graph is a set of vertices (nodes) connected by edges — modeling networks, relationships, and structures. Directed vs undirected, weighted vs unweighted. Degree (edges per vertex). Paths, cycles, connectivity. Trees (connected, acyclic graphs — the structure of hierarchies and many algorithms). Key problems: shortest path (Dijkstra's algorithm — GPS navigation), spanning trees (minimum-cost networks), graph coloring (scheduling, map coloring), Euler and Hamiltonian paths. Graphs model social networks, the internet, molecules, logistics — everything connected.

WORKED EXAMPLE: GPS finds the fastest route by modeling roads as a weighted graph (intersections = vertices, roads = edges, travel time = weights) and running Dijkstra's shortest-path algorithm. Every time your phone navigates, it's solving a graph theory problem. The same algorithms route internet packets, optimize deliveries, and rank web pages — graph theory is the mathematics of connection.

title: Algorithms & Complexity
content:
KEY CONCEPTS: An algorithm is a step-by-step procedure. Analyzing efficiency: Big-O notation describes how runtime grows with input size — O(1) constant, O(log n) logarithmic, O(n) linear, O(n log n), O(n²) quadratic, O(2ⁿ) exponential. Recursion (functions calling themselves) and its relation to induction. Divide-and-conquer, dynamic programming, greedy algorithms. Complexity classes: P (efficiently solvable) vs NP (efficiently checkable). The P vs NP question asks whether these are the same — the most important open problem in computer science, unsolved, with strong evidence they differ.

WORKED EXAMPLE: Searching a sorted list of 1 million items: linear search checks up to 1,000,000; binary search (halving each step) checks only ~20 (log₂ of a million). This is the difference between O(n) and O(log n) — for large inputs, algorithmic efficiency matters more than faster hardware. A better algorithm beats a faster computer, which is why complexity analysis is central to computer science.

title: Grandmaster — Boolean Algebra, Automata & Computation
content:
KEY CONCEPTS: Boolean algebra (variables that are 0 or 1, with AND/OR/NOT) is the mathematics of digital circuits — every computer chip implements Boolean logic in silicon. Logic gates build from it. Finite automata and state machines model computation and pattern recognition (regular expressions). The Turing machine defines what is computable at all — some problems (the Halting Problem) are provably impossible for any computer to solve. Formal languages and grammars underpin compilers. Computability theory reveals the fundamental limits of what algorithms can and cannot do.

WORKED EXAMPLE: The Halting Problem asks: can a program determine whether any given program will eventually stop or loop forever? Turing proved this is undecidable — NO algorithm can solve it for all cases. This isn't a limitation of current technology; it's a mathematical impossibility, proving that computation itself has hard boundaries. Some things cannot be computed, no matter how powerful the machine — a profound result at the foundation of computer science.

title: King Level — Discrete Math as the Foundation of Computing
content:
KEY CONCEPTS: At the highest level, discrete mathematics is revealed as the theoretical bedrock of all computing — every algorithm, data structure, database, network, encryption scheme, and AI system rests on it. Logic became digital circuits; graph theory became networks and search; number theory became cryptography; combinatorics became complexity analysis; automata became compilers and programming languages. The deepest results reveal fundamental limits: undecidability (some problems no algorithm can solve), intractability (P vs NP — some problems appear inherently hard), and the boundaries of formal systems (Gödel). The King-level truth: discrete mathematics doesn't just enable computing — it defines its very possibilities and limits. Understanding it means understanding what computers can do, what they cannot do, and why — the conceptual foundation beneath the entire digital world, including the hard limits that no clever engineering can overcome.

WORKED EXAMPLE: When you use a password, cryptography (number theory) protects it; when you search Google, graph algorithms (PageRank) rank results; when your code compiles, automata theory parses it; when a problem is 'too slow,' complexity theory (Big-O, NP-hardness) explains why. Every layer of computing traces to discrete mathematics. And its limit results — the Halting Problem, P vs NP — define hard boundaries: no architecture, however clever, computes the uncomputable or makes NP-complete problems efficiently solvable. Discrete math is both the foundation and the fence.
